note.headline: Apple's Returns on Capital Keep Widening While the Price Runs Ahead of Every Model We Run
why: The June quarter, reported 30 Jul 2026, beat on both lines: earnings per share of US$2.02 against a US$1.89 consensus, a 6.9% surprise, on revenue of US$109.4b that came in 0.3% ahead. That is the thirteenth beat in thirteen scored quarters, a 100% record that says more about how the company guides than about how it trades.

Return on invested capital reached 51.9% against a weighted average cost of capital we put at 8.9% — a spread of 43%, the widest of the ten filed years, and the tenth consecutive year above the hurdle. The average spread across the run is 23.9%. Very few businesses of this size sustain anything close to it.

The shares change hands at US$309.35 against a US$186.53 fair value estimate, a 1.66 price/fair value. Every one of the thirteen models behind that estimate lands below the current price; the most generous, a price/earnings multiple, stops at US$250.97.

Our quant rating is Hold, grade B, 2.89 of 5 across 75 ranked ratios. Profitability carries it at A- and 3.95 while valuation drags at C- and 1.69, and the arithmetic between those two poles is the whole of the rating. This is a top-percentile operating business trading on multiples that rank in the bottom quintile of its own sector.
note.bottomLine: We rate Apple Hold on the quant scale — grade B, 2.89 of 5 across 75 ranked ratios. A profitability score of 3.95 that ranks top-percentile in the Technology sector on every measure of return on capital is pulled back by a valuation score of 1.69, and the composite lands in the middle. We read the business as wide-moat, with ten of ten filed years earning more on capital than that capital cost. Separately, the shares screen overvalued at US$309.35 against a US$186.53 fair value estimate; on a Medium uncertainty band they would read undervalued below US$130.57. Nothing in the operating record argues against this company. The argument is entirely about what has already been paid for it.

strategy: Apple turned over US$466.8b in the trailing twelve months and converted 27.6% of it into net income, employing 166.0k people to do so. The gross margin stands at 48.7% and the operating margin at 33.2%. Those three figures together describe a business that is unusual less for its size than for the fact that scale has not diluted it: the company is roughly twice as large as it was a decade ago and materially more profitable per unit of revenue than it was then.

The revenue mix is concentrated and the concentration is the central fact about the company. iPhone accounts for 50.4% of revenue at US$209.6b, and Service for 26.2% at US$109.2b. Wearables, Home and Accessories contributes 8.6%, Mac 8.1% and iPad 6.7%. More than half of what the company earns therefore depends on one product line, and any forecast for Apple is in large part a forecast for that line and for the installed base it creates.

The second half of that mix matters more than its share suggests. Services revenue is earned off devices already sold, carries no bill of materials, and is the most plausible explanation for a gross margin that has moved from 39.1% in 2016 to 46.9% in 2025. Hardware sold at a premium does not, on its own, widen a margin by nearly eight points across a decade in which component costs and currencies both moved against the industry.

Geographically the business is less concentrated than the product mix. The Americas segment accounts for 42.9% of revenue, Europe 26.7%, Greater China 15.5%, the rest of Asia Pacific 8.1% and Japan 6.9%. The Greater China share is the line most worth watching: it is large enough to matter to consolidated growth and it is the one region where the company faces both a determined domestic competitor set and a policy environment it does not control.

Across the ten filed years to 2025 revenue compounded from US$215.6b to US$416.2b while the operating margin widened from 27.8% to 32%. Research and development spending rose over the same span from US$10.05b to US$34.55b. That is the shape of a company reinvesting heavily and still expanding its margin, which is the combination operating leverage is supposed to produce and very rarely does at this scale.

Looking forward we take the consensus path as filed rather than substituting a house view. The 27 analysts covering the company expect revenue to compound at 7.6% a year and earnings per share at 11.5% through 2029, off net income growth of 11%. The gap between the earnings and the per-share line is the buyback, and it has been worth roughly a point and a half a year. We note the vendor's outer years are not monotonic as coverage thins; the tail is used unsmoothed and should be read as an estimate, not a plan.
bulls: Return on invested capital of 51.9% has exceeded our estimate of the cost of that capital in ten of the last ten filed years, by an average of 23.9% and by 43% in the most recent one — a record of value creation that almost nothing of this size matches.

The services line now contributes 26.2% of revenue at US$109.2b, and the shift toward it has lifted the gross margin from 39.1% to 46.9% across the filed run while the operating margin widened from 27.8% to 32%.

The balance sheet converts: operating cash flow covers total debt 1.74 times and free cash flow covers it 1.62 times, both top-percentile in the sector, with net debt at just 0.3x EBITDA and an Altman Z-score of 12.49.
bears: The valuation is the whole of the bear case and it is not marginal: 42.3x book ranks in the bottom 4% of the Technology sector, and against a US$186.53 fair value estimate the shares trade at a 1.66 price/fair value — every one of the thirteen models lands below the market price.

Half the business is one product: iPhone is 50.4% of revenue, and a further 15.5% of consolidated revenue is earned in Greater China, so two concentrations that can move together account for a large share of the forecast.

The balance sheet is efficient rather than conservative — a current ratio of 1.00 ranks in the bottom 9% of the sector and equity funds just 28% of assets, in the bottom 14%, both consequences of returning more cash than the business generates.
moat: We assign Apple a wide economic moat rating. Return on invested capital has exceeded our estimate of the company's weighted average cost of capital in ten of the last ten filed years, by an average of 23.9%. In the most recent year the spread was 43% — return on invested capital of 51.9% against a cost of capital of 8.9% — and it is the widest of the run. A record that consistent is not the product of a good decade in an end market. Something is defending it.

What that something is, on the evidence available here, is the combination of a device business that commands a price premium and a services business earned off the devices already in circulation. Services are 26.2% of revenue at US$109.2b and require no unit to be manufactured. That is the mechanism by which the gross margin moved from 39.1% to 46.9% across the filed run, and it is also why the margin is unusually stable: the standard deviation of gross margin across those ten years is 3.5%.

Margin stability of that order through a decade containing a pandemic, a component shortage and a substantial currency cycle is itself the evidence. A price-taker's gross margin moves with its input costs. This one did not, which says the company has not had to buy its volume, and pricing power held through a full cycle is the most durable form of competitive advantage there is.

A word on which return figure to read. Return on equity is 137.2% and return on assets 33.6%, both top-percentile, but the first of those is substantially flattered: a decade of buybacks has left equity funding only 28% of assets, and a thin equity base lifts return on equity without the business improving at all. Return on invested capital, at 51.9%, counts debt and equity alike and is the honest read. It is the one we rate the moat on.

What would erode it is visible in the same numbers. Half of revenue sits in a single product line, and a moat that rests on an ecosystem is only as durable as the reason to stay inside it. Reinvestment has been heavy — research and development rose from US$10.05b to US$34.55b across the run — which is consistent with a company that understands the position has to be defended rather than merely harvested, but heavy spending is a cost of the moat and not proof of it.

The stated limit on this rating matters more than usual here. Morningstar's wide rating is a forecast that excess returns persist for twenty years. This one is a measurement of ten years that have already happened, and no arithmetic over filed accounts can make the forward claim. A company whose advantage is about to be competed away still measures wide on this evidence. Read it as the record a moat rating would be built from, not as the rating itself.
fairValue: Our fair value estimate is US$186.53 a share. It is the median of thirteen independent models — seven discounted cash flow and six relative multiples — which span US$26.93 to US$250.97. The middle half of them sits between US$140.71 and US$224.01, a band 44.7% wide against the estimate, and it is that band rather than the full span that feeds the Medium uncertainty rating.

At US$309.35 the shares trade on 35.3x trailing earnings and 35x forward, on an enterprise value of 27.2x EBITDA, for a free cash flow yield of 3%. That is a 1.66 price/fair value. The more useful way to put it: every one of the thirteen models lands below the traded price, and the most generous of them — a price/earnings multiple applied to forward earnings — stops at US$250.97.

The low end of the range should be discounted rather than averaged in. The price/book model returns US$26.93, which is not a statement about Apple but about the method: book value is a small and shrinking number for a company whose diluted share count has fallen 31.8%, and any multiple of it is meaningless here. That is the case for taking the median of thirteen views rather than the mean, and for publishing the range rather than a point.

The estimate is most sensitive to the terminal assumption and to the discount rate, in that order. The consensus path it rests on — revenue compounding at 7.6% and earnings per share at 11.5% through 2029, from 27 contributing analysts — is not aggressive. What separates US$186.53 from US$309.35 is not the next four years of growth but what is assumed after them, and a 3% free cash flow yield against a cost of equity we estimate at 9.1% is the compact version of the gap.

None of this is a forecast that the price will converge. The analyst price target consensus sits at US$340.72, 10.1% above the current price, which is a fair reminder that a fair value estimate and a price target are different instruments answering different questions. The models here ask what the cash flows are worth; a target asks where the stock will trade.

No fair value on this page feeds the quant rating. The separation is deliberate: a valuation is a set of assumptions the reader chooses, and letting a chosen assumption move a sector-relative rating would make that rating mean something different for every reader. The valuation zone is the one place a fair value is used, and it is labelled as such.
risk: We assign Apple a Medium uncertainty rating, built from six of six measurable drivers. Only one of them reads wide: the spread across the valuation models, at 44.7% between the upper and lower quartile. The other five are contained or moderate, which is what places the rating in the middle of the scale rather than above it.

Taking them in turn: share price volatility of 25.1%, annualised from weekly returns over the past year, reads moderate. Beta of 1.09 is contained — the shares move with the market rather than ahead of it. Net debt of 0.3x EBITDA is contained by any standard. Net margin variability of 9.9% against its own average is contained, and consensus dispersion of 0.5% between the high and low estimate for the current year is very tight indeed.

That last figure is worth pausing on. Twenty-seven analysts arriving within half a percent of each other on next year's earnings is not a sign that the future is knowable; it is a sign that this company guides carefully and that the sell side has learned to follow the guidance. The 100% beat rate across thirteen scored quarters is the same fact seen from another angle. Neither tells you anything about the years the guidance does not cover.

The company-specific concentrations are the risks the drivers above do not capture. iPhone is 50.4% of revenue and Greater China is 15.5%, and those exposures are not independent of each other. The shares have already fallen 13.8% peak to trough inside the last year, and have returned 36.2% over twelve months while lagging the sector by 3.8% — a reminder that the recent move has been the market's more than the company's.

The honest limit on this rating is what the method cannot see. Morningstar sets its equivalent from an analyst's scenario analysis of the business. This one is measured from market and accounting data, which catches a volatile, geared or hard-to-forecast company reliably and will miss anything that has not yet appeared in the numbers: a regulatory decision on the App Store economics, an adverse ruling on the default-search arrangements, a supply chain interruption, a product transition that does not take. None of those would move a single driver above until after the fact.
capital: We assign Apple a Standard capital allocation rating, scoring 4.0 of 6 across the three legs. The balance sheet reads adequate, investment exceptional, and shareholder distributions adequate. The middle leg is the one carrying the rating, and the two adequates are both consequences of the same deliberate policy rather than of any weakness in the business.

On the balance sheet, the company holds US$62.38b of cash against US$84.28b of total debt, leaving net debt at 0.3x EBITDA. The Altman Z-score is 12.49 and the Piotroski score 9 of 9, both about as strong as those screens go. What pulls the leg to adequate rather than sound is the current ratio of 1.00, which ranks in the bottom 9% of the sector, and equity funding just 28% of assets. This is a balance sheet run for efficiency, not for comfort.

The investment leg is where the rating is earned. Returns on capital sit 43% above their cost in the latest year and have averaged 23.9% above across the ten-year run. Research and development spending rose from US$10.05b to US$34.55b over that period while the operating margin widened from 27.8% to 32% — reinvestment at scale that has not diluted the returns it was funded from. There is no evidence here of capital being deployed into anything that earns less than it costs.

Distributions are large and consistent. The company returned US$106.1b to shareholders in the most recent filed year through dividends and buybacks combined, and the diluted share count has fallen 31.8% across the run. The dividend itself is a rounding error by comparison — a 0.3% yield on a 12.1% payout ratio — which makes the buyback effectively the entire distribution policy.

That US$106.1b represented 107.5% of free cash flow, and returning more than the business generated in the year is why the leg reads adequate rather than appropriate. It is not imprudent at this level of net debt and it is plainly accretive while returns on capital run at 51.9%: retiring stock funded at the margin by cheap debt, in a company earning five times its cost of capital, is arithmetic that works. It is worth naming as policy rather than as a one-off, because it is also the reason the current ratio and the equity base look as thin as they do.

One thing this rating does not assess is management. Timothy D. Cook leads the company, and tenure, succession, the judgement behind an acquisition and the quality of the board are not in the filings this report reads. Morningstar's equivalent rating rests heavily on exactly those. Ours rests on three measured legs and claims nothing beyond them.
